The student said, "Xinghua said, 'I borrow Your Majesty’s treasure to look at it. What about that? The Master said, "A phoenix is born on the Cinnabar Mountain;
the *shao* music resounds in the Golden Hall. The student said, "The Emperor lifts the feet of his head-wrap with both hands.
Is this to reveal it before the throne, or to cover it over? The Master said, "Heaven and earth cannot contain it; Yao and Shun do not know it."
The monk named Jin said, "When a dragon finds water, its spirit increases; when a tiger encounters mountain scenery, its ferocity grows.
The Master said, "Be careful not to poke and prod recklessly. Jin asked, "As for Xinghua’s saying, 'Who dares to appraise the King's treasure?
what about that? The Master said, "A single word cuts off the mouths of a thousand rivers; only before a ten-thousand-fathom peak does one attain the profound. The monk [departed].
After the prostrations, the Master said: "The Sage established the Ultimate, his radiance shattering the myriad realms. The August Heaven is impartial; it assists only virtue.
Thus, the sages of past and present share the same sagely virtue in their illumination; the Buddhas of antiquity and today are one in mind in their wondrous clarity.
To shed light once more upon this final age and turn the Wheel of Dharma again, he proclaims the ancestral style of old, never falling into decline."
At this juncture, the path is such that clouds move and rain falls, and water reaches its destination to form a channel.

Not only do the springs and rocks increase in brilliance, but both humans and devas are filled with joy. A single phrase encompasses the five thousand-plus scrolls; ten thousand functions respond instantaneously as one becomes luminous from every side.
A pure breeze pervades the earth, and a bright sun shines in the sky. A single path is empty yet solid, standing apart in radiant glory. This is precisely [what is meant by]...
"How is it at such a time? "Within the realm, the sun and moon hang horizontally and vertically; beyond the square, heaven and earth roll up and unroll as they please.
The Master further cited Huanglong’s verse on returning from the city: "When departing, a stream of flowing water saw me off; Returning, a valley full of white clouds welcomed me.
In one body, going and staying are neither going nor staying; Two things that are insentient seem to possess sentience. The Master said:
"Will the great assembly return? Simply practice the matter of equality; what need is there to inquire about one's future path? Take care.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Wuzu Heshang, who said: "At the very end, most earnestly: my house is new in every place.
Within the *daqian* (trichiliocosm) of sand-grains, one cannot avoid being among those people. But tell me, which one is that person among them? [He pointed to] the end of the level marshes.

"This is the green mountain; the traveler is further beyond the green mountain. The Master said, "Although the old man Wuzu mixed mud with water, therein the black and white were most clearly distinguished.
I, however, am not like this: when we meet, I treat you with courtesy."
There is nothing old and nothing new. A peach pit from a thousand years ago, when cracked open, is entirely the person of former times.
Speaking in this manner, tell me: is it the same or is it different? Descend from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Mind after mind does not know one another; dharma after dharma does not reach one another. One phrase settles heaven and earth;
a thousand differences are all cut off at once. Have you not seen how Layman Pang said: 'Originally, I have no mind toward the myriad things;
what prevents the myriad things from constantly surrounding me? The iron ox fears not the lion’s roar; it is just like a wooden man seeing flowers and birds. The body of the wooden man..."
Originally they are without emotion; when flowers and birds encounter people, they are not startled. When the mind and its objects are in suchness, that is it.
Why worry that the path to Bodhi will not be accomplished? Even so, when examined closely, there is still a lack of awakening.
This mountain monk also has a verse: "Always apply the mind in all places; the myriad phenomena before one’s eyes are entirely submerged. A lion at the gate...
The Patriarch roars; Bodhidharma’s face is three inches thick. Carrying his single sandal, he departs for the Western Heaven.
Xuan knows the place where Wuzhuo’s whole body dwells. Beyond the Pamir Mountains, he meets Song Yun. Oṃ maṇi dāri hūṃ phaṭ.
The Head Monk was invited to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "I do not ask about the eyes of humans and devas; from where did the Great Canon and the Small Canon come?
The Master said, "A rootless staff and a pair of worn-out straw sandals. The monk bowed. The Master then said:
"To open the eyes of humans and devas, to display the nostrils of the monastics, to expound a Great Canon, and to reveal boundless wonders."
The meaning is this: if you raise one, you cannot raise two; if you let one point pass by, you fall into the second. Once every three thousand years the Yellow River clears;
five hundred years in the human realm is but a single day and night in that heaven. Now tell me:

what Dharma did Maitreya preach to the five billion devas so that they immediately realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? Have you not heard it said: "The Brahma-sound is pure"?
Elegant. It causes people to delight in hearing it.

He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is it like when the water is cut off and the wheel is stopped? The Master said, "The shrimp cannot leap out of the bucket. The monk pressed further: "How about..."
"If it is thus, then one labors in vain. The Master said, "Cut off your ears and lie in the street. The monk asked, "Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "There is.
The monk asked, "What is the matter that is further above? The Master said, "No need to hang up the stone mirror;
when dawn breaks, all is clear by itself. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "A single film over the eye causes empty flowers to swirl before it."

A fall! Sitting and cutting off all manifold distinctions—pointing directly at one, striking decisively at two. It is like throwing a sword into the air; there is no question of whether it reaches its mark or not.
This is the traceless whirling of the void, where the edge of the blade remains unimpaired. Looking at a form in a mirror is not difficult to see;
grasping the moon in water—how could one ever pick it up? [He] struck his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "I recall a monk asking Xiangyan, 'When one does not admire the sages and does not prize one's own spiritual essence, what then?
Xiangyan replied, 'All myriad functions cease; even the thousand sages cannot carry one away. What is the meaning of this? The Master said:

"The sea is vast, yet fish and dragons are few; the mountains are deep, yet strange creatures abound. The monk pressed further: "Why did Shushan refuse to acknowledge Xiangyan? The Master said: [He remained silent.]
The young master in brocade robes is drunk; the man of the Way beneath the forest trees is sorrowful.

The student asked, "As for Shushan’s saying, 'When the myriad functions have ceased, there is still something remaining; though a thousand sages do not carry it, it is nonetheless obtained from others'—what about that?
The Master said, "A head three feet long. The student asked, "Xiangyan said, 'Uncle, can you not speak? Shushan said, 'I can speak. Xiangyan said..."
Yanli asked the same question as before. Shanshan said, "Why do you not say that 'accepting' and 'agreeing' cannot be taken in their entirety?
Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, "The mud underfoot is deep. Yanli pressed further, saying, "Xiangyan said, 'If you accept, what is it you accept? If you agree, to whom do you agree?'"
Shushan said, "To say 'yes' is to agree with all the sages; to say 'no' is to acknowledge one's own spiritual nature. Why then did he not accord with Xiangyan?
The Master said, "The ox-head faces south, the horse-head faces north. [The student] asked, "Xiangyan said, 'Even if you were to do so, you would still have thirty years of vomiting upside down.
Does this mean there is an echo within words, or is it simply the natural way of things? The Master said:
"Grass grows upon his tongue. The student continued, "Later, Shushan indeed suffered from vomiting.
In the twenty-seventh year [of his life], he said, 'My elder brother Xiangyan predicted that I would vomit while standing at thirty; now twenty-seven years have passed, with three years remaining.
He then used his hand to scrape food from his mouth to fulfill that prediction. The student asked, "And what about this? The Master said, "A sword cuts it off."
The head of the steamer-man; the Persian waist does not bend. [Zhaozhou] said, "Suppose someone were to ask the Master this very day:
'When one does not admire the various sages and does not value one's own spiritual essence, what then? I wonder, Master, with what will you respond?
The Master said, "The staff is not here. [Zhaozhou] said, "Not seeking the essential meaning within words and phrases—only now do I recognize that which cuts off the flow."
The Master said, "One must even vomit [one's understanding] upside down before it can be attained. The monk bowed, and the Master continued: "In the scriptures it is said:
'If there is one person who departs from the source with true awakening, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish. The Patriarchs say:
'If there is one person who departs from the source with true awakening, the empty space of the ten directions will strike and bump against them. In this, Kaiyuan has a living path."

"Accompanying you all on this journey," he said, striking the meditation seat and adding, "A gust of west wind arrives; two or three leaves fall. On the occasion of the end of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said:
"Today is the fifteenth day of the seventh month. [Holding up his staff,] he drew a line with it and said: 'This cuts off the path of complications;
let us proceed freely throughout the world, avoiding the scattering of sand and dust. Why is this so? It is because I—"
"Within the King's treasury, there is no such sword.
Ascending the hall, he manifests the Jewel-King Buddha-land upon the tip of a single hair; sitting within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
The Vajra Deity joins his palms and tramples the broken sand-pot to pieces. Descending from the seat.
He invited the Head of the Rear Hall to ascend the hall. Holding up his staff, he said: "To let one move aside is to fall into the secondary.

He split open Linji’s Three Mysteries and brought forth the very core of the patch-robed monk. Expounding the Dharma of Mahāyāna, he transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
He planted the staff and said: "With every movement, he reveals the ancient path; he does not fall into the trap of the abrupt mechanism."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised this case: A monk asked Dizang, "The character is not formed by one stroke; it is not the character 'eight. I wonder what character it is?
Dizang replied, "Look at the footnote below. The Master said, "Excellent, great assembly! With the ancients, it was like wind blowing across water; patterns formed naturally.
If it were nowadays, people would look only at the main text—what connection would that have? It is just like a mountain..."
When the monk reported it thus, [Dongshan] asked, "And how about this? After a long silence, he said: "The good root is common to all under heaven.
Why not know that the guest holds the torch? It would be better to shatter one's body into fine dust than ever to blind the eyes of a single sentient being."
In front are Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; behind are Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. To the left is the horse-faced ātman (āpāṅga);
to the right is the ox-headed jailer. Amidst the flames in the center, he preaches the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time stand upon the ground and listen. If you can understand this, then host and guest interchange, the ordinary and the sage intersect, and coming and going in birth and death are like wandering through a garden.
If you do not understand, there is no one living in the broken house; let the wild fires burn it as they will.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the fifteenth day of the ninth month. How many practitioners of Zen are acting with such recklessness!
They know only that "from of old until now," yet how could they understand becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor? This mountain monk, unable to restrain his impatience, points out India and this land.
Setting aside for a moment the matter of gathering up the entire world and placing it upon the eyelashes of you all—Master Mazu said: "From..."
"Since the time of the Hu-luan [disorder] thirty years ago, there has been no shortage of salt and sauce. But how about this? 'In pure poverty one always finds joy;

in turbid wealth there is much sorrow. He ascended the hall and said: "What business is there in speaking of Buddhas and Patriarchs? To speak of long and short is already to fall into error. Nevertheless..."
Thus it is. When the wind does not come, the tree does not move. Long standing; take care. On the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises by relying on conditions. Now that this festival has arrived, we pray to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
The Master said, "Entering the water to see the tall man. The monk stepped forward and said, "In my youth, I enjoyed the moon at the edge of the sky; now, in my decline..."
[The Master] said, "Come and look at the flowers in the field of vision. The Teacher said, "Without experiencing one thing, one does not grow one wisdom.

[The Student] asked, "Before the Buddhas and Patriarchs were born, it was difficult to distinguish between clear and turbid phrases. The Teacher said, "The heavy barrier is easy to cross; the bird-path is difficult to traverse.

[The Student] asked, "In that case, you have cut off the vital ford so that not even a drop of water can pass through. The Teacher said, "A fierce tiger hides in the deep mountains; in the shallow..."
The dew on the grass reveals the multitude of snakes. The monk prostrates. The Master then says: "One is three; three is one. The stone sprout secretly sends forth its branches;
the reed-ash feels the return of the seasonal laws. This wondrous function, manifest in all directions, is truly pitiable—nothing compares to the reality of the mind.
He strikes the meditation staff and says: "I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Yunmen, who said: "The old masters of antiquity all spoke 'talk that descends into the weeds' out of compassion, so that one might recognize people according to their words.
As for 'talk that emerges from the weeds,' it is not like this. If it were like this, there would be talk of double-meaning interpretations.
The Master said: "Fufu is not so. If there were a single phrase that reached you, your eyebrows and whiskers would fall off."
Not a single word reaches you. [The character for "earth" (土) / "blessing" (祝)] strikes and bumps against it. Hares and horses have horns; oxen and sheep have no horns.
Yangqi has a donkey that has only three legs.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month. A single song from Yunmen transcends both past and present.
It is better to sing the Song of Great Peace, where the myriad phenomena and all things dance together. Within light there is darkness; do not perceive it through the lens of darkness alone.
When there is darkness, there is light; do not meet with light. "O Great Assembly, you thought this was a song of great peace, but it turns out to be the *Cantong qi*.
On the occasion of the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and cited Master Wuzu: "The first day of the year begins the reign; all things are renewed. Last year..."
Begging for fire, one obtains it with the smoke; today, carrying water, one returns with the moon. The movement of the celestial sphere shifts; the winter solstice has arrived.

Before the window, there is a direct path, yet no one is willing to set foot upon it. It is still cold in the first month of spring. May you, the Head Seat and the entire assembly, enjoy ten thousand blessings in your daily lives.
Su Wu joyfully tended sheep by the seaside for many days; Li Ling gazed toward the Han Terrace from the borderlands.
A laugh breaks out at dawn; where does it land? Human righteousness is entirely severed at the point of poverty, while worldly sentiments tend to lean heavily toward the wealthy.
The Master said: "Although the old man Wuzu provides blessings in accordance with the times, he cannot help but be biased and one-sided regarding matters."
I, this mountain monk, am not like that. At the commencement of the new year, all things are renewed. A tower near the water gains the moonlight first;

flowers and trees facing the sun easily encounter spring. As the movements of the sun's shadow shift, the days grow longer at the winter solstice. Thus, peach-wood talismans are nailed upon the gates.

This humble sister-dharma-laywoman does not dare to enter. It is still cold during the first month of spring. I respectfully wish that the Head Seat and the entire assembly each enjoy ten thousand blessings in your daily lives.
May you enter this new year with all matters being most auspicious. [The speaker] descends from the seat.
The Buddha ascends the hall for the occasion of his *parinirvāṇa*. "The Buddha’s body is unconditioned; it does not fall within the realm of numerical reckoning.
Old Śākyamuni has entered *parinirvāṇa*. Fire breaks out in the Nairañjanā River, burning Mount Sumeru.

He struck the meditation seat and said, "Why do you press people so hard?
Upon receiving the news of the passing of Master Dongzhou of Tiger Hill, he ascended the hall and said: "The crown of all sages, a single point that the myriad spirits cannot grasp.
It cuts through nails and severs iron, shaking heaven and earth; with a swift step, it tramples over the pit of birth and death. This is Tiger Hill."
In the hall sat the Venerable Dongzhou; for fifty-eight years, he could not be caged nor called back.

His inexhaustible phrases—where the sharp edge had not yet been revealed, the literary brilliance was fully manifest; where black and white were not yet distinguished, he acted with independent liberation at every opportunity.
Thus, dwelling in mountains across five locations, his Dharma encompassed the entire realm; preaching at six assemblies, his fame spread throughout the monastic groves.
Master Lin, having completed his duties, suddenly returned to the truth. His final barrier was so secure that not even a drop of water could pass through it.

Thus it is said: "When he lifts [the whisk], lightning strikes and thunder roars; when he lets it down, the sky is clear and the sea is still. When asked, "What is it like when neither lifting nor letting down?
after a long silence, he said: "Thirty years hence."

"If there were even one dharma that surpassed nirvana, I would say it is likewise like a dream and like an illusion. Descend from your seats.

Its fragrance spreads to the eight directions; where it is burned, the harmonious breath of the myriad states prevails.

The direct cause [of this] is the adamantine and solid physical body, which realizes a lifespan as boundless as space.

On the day of the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a competitive boat race. Eye meets eye; heart connects with heart.

They display their oars and dance with their paddles without disturbing a single ripple. Emerging and submerging, rolling up and unfolding, they vie for the first place to behold the prize. The silken banner is won by one alone."
Seizing the moment, with songs and chants filling the road, he turns the prow of his boat and returns home to sit in peace.
Thus, Master Longya said: "To study the Way, one must first have an awakening; it is like once having raced a swift dragon boat.
Though it is but an old hall and empty ground, only after winning it once does one finally rest. Rest! Rest! Within the palaces of the Dragon King, not a single person is seen wandering."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Great wisdom is not illumination; true emptiness leaves no trace. Two hundred monks are spinning around in confusion;
among them, perhaps one or two do not allow themselves to be deceived. Danchu, for this entire summer, I have not spoken in vain with you all, whether east or west.
But in the end, what is it? Nanquan slaughtered the cat."
Departing for Baoning, he took his leave of the assembly and ascended the hall to speak: "Going and staying are fundamentally without sentiment; The official vessel hastens my departure.
The breeze is clear in the Chamber of Ambrosia; The tide fills the City of Stone Walls. The Way of the Patriarchs is as distant as heaven; The Imperial Grace is as level as the sea.
I intend to pour forth my very liver and gall, Like the sunflower and mugwort inclining toward the sun."

"Regarding the great matter of the Zen school, since the time of Nanyue and Mazu, and following Linji and Deshan, there have been countless variations and distinctions—transcending lineages and surpassing conventional standards. Like a jade... [text fragment].

The turning of the bead has been preserved in full within the volumes of the scriptures. Yet, Master Xuedou, having opened wide the natural eye of wisdom, gave unrestrained discourse on the mysteries beyond the conventional.

Regarding his methods of responding to and examining cases, as well as his deployment of expansion and contraction, or concession and seizure, he is considered the foremost of all time by both ancient and modern scholars.

While students merely know to revere him, they have not yet fully grasped the ultimate intent of his teachings; were it not for his compassionate descent [to guide us], [this essence would remain hidden].
[The Master] developed [the teaching] and made his principles manifest. How can later students thoroughly understand them? The Master said:

"When the masters of our school are driven by necessity, they offer a single word or half a phrase, valuing only that one may directly realize one's homecoming. How could there be any room for intellectual understanding of the profound and subtle, or for you to claim you have 'grasped' it?
Students themselves lack wondrous awakening and cannot penetrate through to see the source. They inherit the words but lose the essence."

They stagnate in words and become lost in the ultimate meaning; relying on others, they form their own interpretations. They cling to established tracks and follow conventional paths, so that when faced with the critical moment, they know not how to act.
Yet, as for a mirror, it possesses no active power to illuminate images; it is simply empty and pure. I have long been ill at ease with the practice of secret, room-to-room transmission.
To peddle the words of the ancients without grounding oneself in the fundamental vehicle of the Dharma is utterly deceptive. What you have requested is by no means a trivial matter;
it is merely that my own writing is so coarse and crude that I am insufficient to follow in the noble tracks of the former sages.

Consequently, the Master then re-presented one hundred ancient cases cited by Xuedou, recording them as they were attained. Once this massive volume was completed, he did not dare to keep it for private use.
To broaden my learning and insight is truly my aspiration; therefore, I have recounted the origins of this matter and placed them at the beginning of this volume.

The Sixth Patriarch asked: "A śramaṇa possesses the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. From where have you come, Venerable One?"

As he was approaching, [Nanyue] gave rise to great arrogance. Xuedou said, "Had he been able to let out that one shout at that moment, we would not have seen this case of a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail.
He then raised the story again: [Nanyue] circumambulated the meditation seat three times, struck his staff once, and stood there with a resolute air.
On behalf of the Patriarch, Xuedou said, "Before you had even reached Caoxi, I would have given you thirty blows!"
The Master said: "When Yongjia had not yet reached Caoxi, he was full of self-important spirit; but once he arrived, it was as if he were pushing a cart through mud—struggling at every step.

Although Xuedou, in the place where host and guest interchange, reveals his superior claws and fangs, if one examines him closely, he cannot avoid being buried in a ditch or filling a ravine. [He struck with the master’s staff.]
With a single stroke he said: "The patriarchs and ancestors could not resolve it; the calamity has reached their descendants.
He cited Yangshan, who pointed to a snow lion and asked, "Is there anyone who can pass through this color?
Yunmen said, "At that time, I would have pushed it over. Xuedou said, "He only knows how to push it over; he cannot lift it up."
The Master said: "To knock it down and then lift it up; there is guest and there is host. Buying a hat to fit the head; a tall man entering the water.
He then cited Xiangyan’s "Hanging Words": "It is like a person climbing a tree, with a branch held in his mouth, neither grasping a branch with his hands nor treading on a branch with his feet.
If someone below the tree asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, not to answer would be to disregard their question; yet if one does answer..."
To lose one’s body and life—at such a moment, what is it? There was a Venerable Head-Tiger who said, "I do not ask about having climbed the tree;
please, Master, speak before one has climbed it. Yanguan laughed heartily. Xuedou said, "It is easy to speak from atop the tree;
it is difficult to speak beneath the tree. Even this old monk would climb the tree to bring forth a question."
The Master said: "I, this mountain monk, am not like that. Whether on top of a tree or beneath a tree, I say it is altogether not difficult.
But tell me: to support Xiangyan, or to support Houtou?
Consider this case: A monk asked Luzu, 'What is the speech that is not spoken? Luzu replied, 'Where is your mouth?'"
The monk said, "I have no mouth. The Patriarch asked, "What do you use to eat your meals? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou said, "A good opportunity for a blow across the back! Such fellows: once they open their mouths, they cannot close them; once they close their mouths, they cannot open them."
The Master said, "Having no mouth, what food would one eat? Xuedou said, "If you open your mouth, you cannot close it; if you close your mouth, you cannot open it.
To err by a hair's breadth is to lose the mark by a thousand li."
A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Feng said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom.

The monk asked, "What of those who drink from it? Feng said, "It does not enter through the mouth. The monk took this up and presented it to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "It cannot enter through the nostrils.
The monk then asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter."
When asked, "What about one who drinks? Zhaozhou said, "Dead. Upon hearing this, Xuefeng remarked, "Zhaozhou is an ancient Buddha," and from that time on, he no longer answered questions.
Xuedou said, "Everyone in the assembly says that Xuefeng did not answer the monk’s question; therefore, Zhaozhou refused to acknowledge him.
To interpret the matter in such a way is a profound disservice to the ancients. Xuedou, however, is not like this—he cuts through nails and severs iron."
"The masters of the fundamental division [of the school] find it difficult to act as authors when leveling the high with the low.
The Master said, "If it is so, then grass bows and wind blows; if it is not so, then one draws a snake and adds feet.
I, this mountain monk, say that both Xuefeng and Zhaozhou have been thoroughly pierced through by this monk. How can this be seen? From this point on, Xuefeng...
He did not answer.

[The Master] raised a case where a monk asked the West Hall Master (Xitang): "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined. But what about when there is neither question nor answer?
The Master said, "I am afraid it will rot right there. A monk asked Changqing: "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined..."
"However, what is it like at a time when there is neither question nor answer? Jing said, "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office;
yet who has ever seen a single person beneath the forest trees? Xuedou said, "Why not give him his proper fodder?"
The Master said: "I thought the monkey was white; there is also a black monkey. Suddenly, someone asked the mountain monk:

"When there is a question and an answer, the guest and host are clearly distinct. But when there is neither question nor answer, how is it? He simply replied: "One draws out three, two adds four. "Ultimately, how is it? [He said:
"Fan Kuai’s rage before the Hall of the High Ancestor."
Linzhi addressed the assembly, saying: "At my former teacher’s place, I received sixty blows three times; it was like being brushed with a bundle of mugwort.
Now I am thinking of having one more meal—who will step forward to deal the blow? A monk came forth from the assembly and said, "I shall deal the blow.
Linzhi took up his staff and gave it to the monk; as the monk prepared to receive it, Linzhi struck him. Xuedou said: "Linzhi’s way of letting go was superior."
Dangerous! He was brought back too quickly.
The Master said: "The patriarchs' way of guidance is like a strong man extending his arm; it does not borrow the power of another.
Yet, if one were to examine it closely, there would inevitably be gain and loss. At that time, the monk waited for him to raise his staff.
He brushed out his sleeves and departed immediately. Even for such a man, there was not the slightest need for a lightning-fast wit.
Xuedou said: "Linji’s letting go was perilous; his gathering back was too swift. Has he even finished eating the blow?"

"That is not so. He then held up his fist and said, "When clenched, it is a fist; there is high and low. He then opened his hand and said, "When opened, it becomes a palm;
there is no factionalism and no partiality. Now tell me, is it better to act for others by letting go, or is it better to act for others by holding fast?
To open is to build a carriage; to clench is to fit the tracks. If you say, "Building a carriage inside the gate, one fits the tracks upon leaving," I already know you.
"You are making your living inside a ghost cave.
The Master said, "The two great elders—letting go and holding fast—are entirely not dependent on others.
To examine this closely, it is much like using a shrimp as an eye. I, this mountain monk, am not like that: even when opening, one cannot call it 'holding.'"

Even when grasped, it cannot be called a fist. Without high or low, without faction or partiality, in the kingdom of the Great Yuan Emperor, the transformation of the three thousand worlds continues as before.
A monk asked Muzhou, "What is it like when one bows high to Śākyamuni but does not prostrate to Maitreya?
Muzhou said, "Yesterday someone asked this; I chased him out. The monk said, "I fear, Master, that I am not sincere. Muzhou said, "The staff is not here;
I will give you thirty blows with the handle of a broom. Xuedou said, "Muzhou had only the heart to accept the jade."
Furthermore, he had no intention of dividing the city.

The Master said: "Muzhou held the scales in his hand; his choices were made according to the occasion. Although Xuedou was like a mirror set upon a stand, he seemed much too intent on gazing at the heavens.
I, this mountain monk, am not like that. If someone were to ask me suddenly, I would bow high to the Buddha and [turn away].
Qia asked, "When you do not pay homage to Maitreya, how is that? He replied, "A fierce tiger sits blocking the road.
The Master said, "Are you afraid I am not sincere? He simply said to him, "I suspect you were not made from golden teeth;
how could you have drawn your bow to shoot Wei-chi?"
Zhaozhou pointed to a jujube tree and asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From the land of Han.

Zhaozhou asked, "Does the Emperor of the land of Han still hold the Buddha-dharma in high regard? The monk said, "How tragic! Fortunately you asked me; had you asked someone else, disaster would have ensued.
Zhaozhou asked, "What did he do? The monk replied, "He does not even recognize people; what Buddha-dharma could there be for him to hold in high regard?"
Zhuo said, "How many years have you been ordained, Preceptor? The monk replied, "Twenty summers. Zhuo said, "Very good!
Yet I see no one here," and he struck him. Xuedou said, "This monk deserved the blow; however, once gone, he will not return.
Although Zhuo’s command was carried out, alas, he stirred up waves where there was no wind."
The Master said: "This monk has made a small exit and encountered a great opportunity; the effort spent on the jujube tree was not in vain. Nevertheless, once gone, he will not return;
yet he truly possesses the lot to repay his debt of gratitude. As for those who speak of the Way, they do not even see that there is any Buddha-dharma worth valuing.
Nowadays, people everywhere often argue in terms of gain and loss. Alas! This is the deafness of one who lacks the innate wisdom of a teacher."
It is difficult to distinguish the differences between the *gong* and *shang* notes; only one with the keen vision of Li Zhu can discern the distinction between black and white.
Then, looking around to his left and right, he said: "Is there here any monk of natural character and spirit?"
[The Master] cites Zhaozhou’s question to the old woman: "Where are you going? The woman says, "I am going to steal Zhaozhou’s bamboo shoots.
Zhaozhou says, "What will you do when you encounter Zhaozhou? The woman then gives him a slap, and Zhaozhou stops there.
Xuedou says: "A good slap! But give her two more slaps; even so, there is no place for examination."
The Master said: "Zhaozhou swallowed his breath and suppressed his voice; Xuedou used strength to overpower the weak. This mountain monk discusses the matter with impartiality:
I dare say that both the old woman and Zhaozhou have failed to reach a final resolution."
Regarding Baoshou’s opening of the hall: Sanxing pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou struck him.
Sanxing said, "If you act as a teacher in this manner, you will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou! Baoshou then returned to his quarters.
Xuedou said, "Although Baoshou and Sanxing revealed the treasury of the true Dharma-eye of Linji, they were only able to speak where there was no Buddha."
Venerable Sir, had the monks of that time been true men of substance, as soon as they were pushed out, they would have overturned the meditation seat;
even if Baoshou had deployed his full capacity, he would still have been three thousand li short.
The Master said: "Baoshou and Sansheng, if you wish to reveal the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye of Linji, you must reach such a state.
Why? Because it is the sword that kills and the sword that gives life."
A monk asked Wuye, "What is the Buddha? Wuye said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization. Xuedou said, "He blocks the nostrils.
Another monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu said, "The very mind is the Buddha.
Xuedou said, "He props up the tongue."
The Master said: "Block the nostrils; the heavens are clear and the earth is at peace. Prop up the tongue; cliffs crumble and rocks shatter.
He related the case of a monk who asked Deshan, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? Deshan replied, "What? What?
The monk said, "When the imperial decree summons the flying dragon horse, the lame tortoise sticks out its head. Deshan then stopped speaking. On the following day, Deshan was bathing.
He went out. As the monk passed tea to Shanshan, Shanshan patted the monk’s back once. The monk said, "This old fellow has finally had a flash of realization.
Xuedou said, "Even refined gold must pass through a hundred smeltings; it requires the hammer of one's own fundamental nature.
Since Deshan obstructed the man with himself, this monk was likewise subjected to injustice. He struck a line with his staff and said, "The previous case."
"Let us set this aside for a moment. Where have all the sages of antiquity gone? As the assembly hesitated, the Master struck them all at once.
The Master said: "Xuedou’s eye for discerning dragons and snakes is correct; his mechanism for seizing tigers and rhinoceroses is complete.
Yet, when examined closely, it is still like using a broken awl to probe the earth. Since Deshan has already obstructed others with his own [views], where is the monk who receives [the teaching]?"

Yun said, "Though it is a dead snake, one who knows how to handle it brings it back to life. Who is the master of hand? Please try to discern this.
The Master said, "The Venerable Fu displayed his prowess for a time; having caught it, he immediately went off, yet he still could not get to eat the melon."
Both the Great Xuedou and the Little Xuedou have turned cleverness into clumsiness.
They cite Nanquan’s address to the assembly: "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. Zhaozhou stepped forward and asked, "What is the Way outside of things?
Nanquan struck him. Zhaozhou said, "Master, do not strike me; you will strike the wrong person in the future."

[Zhaozhou] departed. Quan said, "Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; it is difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk. Xuedou said, "Zhaozhou was like a dragon without horns, yet like a snake with feet.
At that time, he did not care that 'exhausting the law leaves no people'; he simply had to be given a beating and driven out."
The Master said: "Zhaozhou was forged entirely of tempered steel; how could he have feared the tongs and hammers?

Although Nanquan acted according to the mandate, he lacked the eyes to see through all quarters. Xuedou said: "At that time, one should not have been concerned with 'exhausting the law lest there be no subjects';
he ought to have been beaten with a staff and driven out. If one has no minor servants at home, one cannot be called a gentleman."
Dongshan was brought before Yunmen. Yunmen asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Dongshan said, "Chadu. Yunmen asked, "Where were you during the summer retreat?
Dongshan said, "Baoci in Hunan. Yunmen asked, "When did you leave? Dongshan said, "The eighth month of last year. Yunmen said, "I grant you three blows of the staff.

"Blinking upward. How can one say that this matter has been missed? A monk asked, "Why do the eyebrows not blink upward?

"Do you understand? General Li has a fine reputation; even if he does not receive a fief, he remains at ease.

The Master replied, "This is merely routine; I do not concern myself with it. The scholar said, "Was it not improper for you to question me just now?

The Master cited a monk asking Yunmen, "What is it like when a single word exhausts the Way? Yunmen said, "Torn asunder. Xuedou snapped his fingers three times.

A monk asked Muzhou, "What is it like when a single word expresses everything? Muzhou said, "The old monk is inside your alms-bag.
Xuedou let out a great laugh.

Consciousness. It is simply called a "fist.

tell me, when Daguang offered the extra tea to that monk, what was he doing?

On this occasion of the summer retreat’s conclusion, I have given this small discourse upon rising from illness. The months and years cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for anyone.

For these past ten days or so, I have been assailed by alternating chills and fevers; I sought the very source of their arising, but could not find it. Why? Because the physical form has detached itself.
Because the mind is like an illusion, once the physical form has departed, the mind is likewise illusory. The nature of the Buddha’s illness and the Patriarchs’ illnesses is the same.
The Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, said: "When illness comes, it clings to the skin and bones; Shake yourself free, and not a single thing remains.
Walking, you cannot take a step; your voice is low; Yet your nostrils remain high and prominent. The Elder of the Fifth Patriarch spoke thus.
It is said: One can only suffer from one's own illness; one cannot cause others to be ill.
Since one cannot cause others to be ill, when one is unable to gather [the conditions] together, one cannot universally enter into the bodies of sentient beings to fully take on their illnesses.

Since one cannot fully take on the illnesses of sentient beings, the karmic consciousness becomes vast and茫然 (vastly bewildered), with no fundamental basis to rely upon. O Great Assembly, within these ninety days, let us be as one in this regard.

Consequently, monks vied with one another to emulate his style and sought from me a eulogy; thus, I wrote them down with rapid brush, composing several pieces.

Hanging a hundred thousand suns together constitutes a single illumination; it reveals the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials. Gathering ten or more peals of thunder constitutes a single shout; it awakens great function and great capacity.
At Huangbo’s staff, the pain penetrates the very marrow of one’s bones; yet one reflects again on that single blow, seeking only personal advantage.
A little ruffian roaming across the world;
the true person without rank; a mask of raw iron; acting like a madman, with no chin and no nose; seizing the tiger’s head and gathering its tail—this cannot be deceived by a minor Śākyamuni.
He neither studies the sutras nor sits in meditation; he has terrified Official Wang Changshi to death.

Huangbo struck him on the cheek with his palm; Dayu rained a fist upon his ribs. At both places, the secure barriers were firmly closed off, leaving the bones exposed and the skin pierced to this day.
Only by beating him to death and cooking him for the dogs to eat would one truly accord with the authentic transmission of Vulture Peak.
Baizhang’s great capacity and Huangbo’s great function—clods of earth and lumps of mud, picked up and displayed as a performance. A thousand peaks reach the mountain;
ten thousand streams flow to the source. While on the road, one does not leave home; while at home, one does not leave the road.
The staff and the shout fly back and forth; illumination and function operate simultaneously. Sages and ordinary folk alike cannot fathom this; he is a "white-handed thief.
With eyes that distinguish dragons from snakes, he burns the meditation boards. Using these several matters to test the monks of the world—this is what is called the True Lineage of Linji.
A tea kettle and a smoothing iron are not the same.
The Ox King met with calamity last night; even until now, no trace of him is seen. Startled, he causes the Three Peaks to stand headlong;
he plays his jade flute crosswise toward the autumn wind.
His mouth is like a foundation stone; his head is like a wooden ladle. Having encountered Huangbo’s sixty blows with the staff, he acts as if no one else exists.
When asked about Zhaozhou’s "Patriarchal Meaning of the Westward Coming," it was just as he happened to be washing his feet—he overturned the great ocean and kicked over Mount Sumeru.
Having consumed the drool and spittle of wild foxes to the full, let him leave his lips unmoved.
The Three Mysteries, the Three Essentials, and the Four Selections; the True Person of No Station at the tips of the hundred grasses.
Every descendant has eyes that stare wide open, yet in the end, they cannot distinguish gold from brass.
Master Huangbo did not study under Dayu; he seized the tiger’s head while simultaneously grasping its tail.
From this point on, he roamed freely throughout the four seas, stirring up windless waves. Puhua was a madman of the winds; together they established the fundamental tenets.
With eyes closed, he leaped across the Yellow River, supporting others as they crossed three thousand li.
Sixty years of tangled resentment with the osier staff—whom does it blame? Light as a mountain, yet heavy as a blade of mugwort.
Not refusing the gold beneath his knees, he went again to Gaoyuan to see Dayu.
The True Man of No Rank protrudes from the gateway of the face; the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was extinguished by the blind donkey.
At the crossroads stands the Stone Daring-to-Be; on his shoulders he carries and in his hands he grasps the board of Muzhou.
Chan Master Fachang Yu’s Eulogy:
The house collapses and the fence crumbles; propped up here and there, it is bare and impoverished. Yet, amidst such poverty, there is world-shaking wealth and honor.
When the Eighteen Patriarchs arrive, let us simply huddle around the hearth and sleep. A winter melon hangs from a gourd vine, scaring the living daylights out of Nan Biantou.
Only then is one a true adept. Zen Master Dahui praised the grasping of the bamboo cane as being neither "back" nor "touch.
He unleashed his single tongue solely to revile Heaven; yet in the end, he could not escape his karmic debt from former lives.

The wooden bow continues the weighty causes and conditions. Amidst the miasmic smoke and pestilential rains of the barbarians, he silently illuminates deviant Chan, sweeping it away until not a hair’s breadth remains.
He rekindles the transmission of Jibei and whips forth seventeen hundred "elephant-dragons," ensuring they do not die at the hands of the blind donkey.
A eulogy for the late Master Yuyang:
He extinguished the seed of the Buddha two thousand years ago; he is the seventeenth-generation descendant of Linji. He filled the valleys and filled the ditches;
he is a dried dung-peg with seven holes and eight apertures, a shattered sand-pot.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Master Tianmu Zhongfeng by Daoqi, the Ruler.
My name has fallen upon the world; thus I offer this eulogy for Zhongfeng. Zhongfeng will say I am insulting him.
With ignorance filling my belly and a wooden board across my entire body, I insult Zhongfeng. Yet Zhongfeng will say I am praising him. Indeed.
Neither reviled nor praised, from the summit of the solitary peak within Tianmu Mountain, he shattered the prison gates of birth and death,
emerged from the delusions of worldly toil, and manifested unlearned wisdom and spontaneous wisdom, writing back the currents of the Nine Rivers and Three Gorges.
Using a splitting arrow and a tiger-trapping trap, he is a dragon-elephant roaming the four seas and five lakes. He is like a bell responding to its strike, or a valley answering an echo.
This is what is called "firmly not dwelling on the mountain" while being able to brilliantly illuminate the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs for a hundred generations—Master Huanzhu.
Self-Praise for the Wondrous Fruit: A Eulogy for National Teacher Nanchu. The portrait was painted on the same scroll and requested with this eulogy.

His practice was not ahead of others, nor did he lag behind; his jaw and cheekbone supported one another, and his openness and obstruction remained in mutual accord. He raised up the broken shards of the sands.
Bowl. Each extends a single hand. Beneath the tall pine tree, before the cascading waterfall and the rocky cliff. A lion roars;
an elephant king circles.
Invited by the Abbot of Yingzang to compose this eulogy.
He does not leap through the vajra-ring, nor does he swallow the thorny burr. In a single flavor, he calls a bell a jar; let him do as he pleases, even if he extinguishes the ancestral style.
Sitting grandly in his place, he allows not even a hair’s breadth of deviation. Last night, on the South Mountain, a tiger bit a tiger.

The Head Seat You has written this mountain-style inscription at the request of Xingzan, who ruined the tradition of Songyuan and extinguished the essential principles of King Yuyang. He refused to acknowledge anything from any other quarters; what kind of core essence does he possess?
He sweeps away the myriad phenomena within the dust and exhausts the great trichiliocosm within a single finger. At the tip of his staff, he possesses ample room to move;

though he has not an inch of length in praising the Buddha-dharma at the request of Elder Huai of Chongbao on the Western Mountain, he manifests a thousand transformations in response to conditions. He directly reveals the total upholding [of the Way], and one may view his hand and face from every direction.
The heavy gates are firmly barred; a single thread is barely passed through. The western mountains roll up their curtains in broad daylight; the true wind of Shaoshi opens its doors.
When Head Monk Mao requested a eulogy, he said:
"To eliminate the 'is' and to eliminate the 'is not,' to sweep away the Three Essentials and the Three Mysteries—this utterly blinds the true eye of Mahesvara. This is it."
Yangqi’s chestnut burr is not like Muzhou’s carrying a wooden board.
At the request of his junior disciple, Chief Seat Yuanhao,
I praise him as he sets out his fishing line before the Ten-Thousand-Fathom Peak and plucks the willow flowers three thousand miles away— this is the patriarch’s single expanse of idle field.
"Earth. Leave it for your descendants to play with as sand and dust.
Wuli Du-si painted a portrait of Master Zeshan and hung it alongside the Master’s own. He requested a eulogy, saying:
"Companions on the Way from forty years ago, we have met three thousand *li* apart. We have exhausted our talk of mountain clouds and sea moons; now we part ways."
North, south, west, and east—the golden cock brushes the jade hare; it strikes the white phoenix and ensnares the fierce dragon.
It expands the vastness of the great void and awakens one to the perfect fusion of ultimate principle. Two mirrors hang high, reflecting all within a single illumination.

The Abbot Zhezang requested a verse on galloping horses atop jagged ice ridges and leaping within the eye of a needle; it does not involve any sense of peril at all, but employs the fodder of one's own fundamental portion.

The marsh is vast, concealing the mountain; its principle can subdue the leopard. Turning the jewel within the Tathāgatagarbha, ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations are all illuminated at once.
—Composed by Sishi Shizhe (思侍侍者) as a request for praise.
Beholding the face while mountains and rivers stand between; east and west are parted and entrusted. Stop up the two roots of the ears and try to hear the drum of lethal poison.
An ancient had this to say: "A great man takes the primordial as the ancestor of his mind."
Master Xiao, Curator of the Archives, requests a verse in praise of Yunmen’s intent in severing the three barriers; he deliberates upon the two shouts of the Jibei (Linji) school.
Not only are the throats of all completely cut off, but both ears are likewise utterly deaf.

At that time, a monk came forward and bowed; Deshan struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have no words..."

[The monk] had not yet asked [a question], so why did he strike him? Shanshan asked, "Where are you from? The monk said, "I am a man from Silla. Shanshan said, "Before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, you deserve thirty blows. It is well to strike him as soon as he emerges to pay his respects; it is well to strike him even before he has stepped onto the boat’s railing. Who else can control his rolling out and withdrawing, his appearing and disappearing?
Those with copper heads and iron jaws are all captured. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, is it perhaps to support Deshan?
The Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, addressed the assembly, saying: "One is three; three is seven. A *nüzhen* flower by the seashore;

a stone of a woman waiting for her husband by the Ju-ma River. The stone strikes red; red earth draws a winnowing fan. Let the eyes be allowed to grow with rheum. He then spoke this verse: One is three, Three is seven, A *nüzhen* flower by the seashore, A stone of a woman waiting for her husband by the Ju-ma River.
The stone strikes red; Red earth draws a winnowing fan. Let the eyes be allowed to grow with rheum. Thus it is said.
The waters are vast and fish tracks are few; the heavens are high and bird prints are rare. Moving my boat across a different inlet, the setting sun lingers faintly over the sandy shore.
A monk asked an ancient master, "What is the eye of a spiritual friend? The master replied, "A paper wick without oil."
The verse says:
Do not worry that the paper wick lacks oil; The hundred rivers still flow toward the east.
Because I see the moon hanging from the tip of a pine branch, I am unaware that the azure sky is above my head.
A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? Lin replied, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains.
The verse says: "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains; A single body amidst heaven and earth. Yesterday's sorrows have already been dispelled; Today, let the face be joyful once more."
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan, said: "The horn of an ox is three inches long; the horn of a rabbit is eight feet long.
The four oceans flow toward the East Sea; Prajñāpāramitā. The verse says:
A snake cannot move without a head; a tiger runs only because it has feet. A large month has thirty days; a small month has twenty-nine.
Master Dongshan addressed the assembly, saying: "Brothers, at the beginning of autumn and the end of summer, some go east and some go west."
"You must go to where there are ten thousand miles and not a single blade of grass before you will succeed.
But as for that place of ten thousand miles and not a single blade of grass—how does one go there? Later, a monk brought this up to Master Shishuang of Liuyang.
Shuangyun said: "Stepping out the door, it is all grass. The verse says:
"Ten thousand miles, not an inch of grass; stepping out the door, it is all grass. Liuyang and Dongshan—one old, one not old."
Have you not seen? The man of Hanshan returned for ten years and could not find his way back; he had forgotten the path by which he came.
The Great Master Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying: "When Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment upon seeing the morning star, a monk stepped forward and asked:
'How was it when Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment upon seeing the morning star?'"
As soon as [Yunmen] entered the gate, he struck him. Master Xianyu raised it first; holding up his whisk, he said, "This is the Hair-tip Star.
He then spoke in verse: A dead inn opened by living men; One buys and sells for oneself. The weights and measures are most distinct; An iron hammer cannot break it.
A monk asked Fengyang, "What is the phrase for receiving a beginner? Fengyang replied, "You are a wandering monk.
The monk asked again, "What is the phrase for discerning a patch-robed monk? Fengyang replied, "The sun rises in the west at dawn."
He asked again, "What is the phrase for the true command being carried out? Yang said, "Bringing it from a thousand miles away to present one's old face.
He asked again, "What is the phrase for settling heaven and earth? Yang said, "In the continent of Uttarakuru, there is long-grained rice;
those who eat it have neither anger nor joy. He then said, "Take these four turning phrases."
To test the monks of the world: as soon as you step forward, they have already tested you. The verse says: Raising my hand, I grasp the Southern Pole;
Lifting my gaze, I look toward the Northern Dipper. Transcending body and mind beyond heaven and earth— Who else is there like me?
Once Yunmen said, "In our school, there is freedom in all directions; killing and giving life are applied according to the occasion.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is killing? Yunmen said, "Winter passes and spring comes. The monk asked, "When winter passes and spring comes, what then?
Yunmen said, "Carrying my staff across my shoulders, I roam the wilds in the south, north, east, and west."
The Stump. The verse says: Winter passes and spring arrives;
yin and yang wax and wane. Killing and giving life are applied according to the occasion; there is no yielding when the opportunity arises.

With the wondrous function of moving freely in all directions, grasses bow like the wind. Leveling the high by descending to the low, one discards three and releases two, roaming the wilds in the north, south, east, and west.
The stump. Carrying the main beam crosswise atop a thousand peaks, Yangshan addressed the assembly, saying:
"One, two, three—my children! With eyes level, look up again. Two mouths with not a single tongue—this is my school’s essential tenet.
The verse says: The stump stands firm; The main beam is carried across the peaks. Eyes level, then looking up; Two mouths, one tongue lacking. This is the Master's intent.

Rabbits and horses have horns; oxen and sheep have no horns. Stone mortars overturn the void; Mount Sumeru stands upside down. A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is it like when the year ends and the time is spent? The worthy said, "The old man Wang of East Village burns paper money at night. The verse says: Rabbits and horses have horns; Oxen and sheep have none. Stone mortars overturn the sky; Mount Sumeru stands on its head. When the year ends and the time is spent, The old man Wang of East Village burns paper money at night.

How could this be grasped by the intellect? It is not something that can be sought through words. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own face. Rabbits and horses have horns; Oxen and sheep have none. Stone mortars overturn the sky; Mount Sumeru stands on its head. When the year ends and the time is spent, The old man Wang of East Village burns paper money at night. How could this be grasped by the intellect? It is not something that can be sought through words. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own face.
The old king of the eastern village burns paper money at night, welcoming the New Year to exchange it for the Old Year. The hornless iron ox sleeps on Mount Shaoshi;
dragged out onto the open ground, he is whipped even more.
The Three Barriers of Huanglong. The verse says:
What is my hand like a Buddha’s hand? Picking up a dustpan and a broom, I sweep away the mist and clouds of the azure void, knocking over the Southern Dipper and the Northern Dipper.
"What are my feet like? They are like donkey's feet! Lost before the ten-thousand-fathom peak. When a wild goat hangs from its horns, there is no trace;
the hunting dog cannot find it. Every person has their own karmic connection; do not debate 'this side' or 'that side. Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch—"
Without going to the Western Heaven, a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body? Yunmen said, "Hide one's body within the Big Dipper.
The verse says:
Lifting [the staff] without looking back—already a miscalculation. Hiding one’s body within the Big Dipper—the hands and feet are already fully exposed. Old Shaoyang is made to laugh to tears;
learning the Tang gait in Handan.
The verse for the offering at the Assembly of Ten Thousand Buddhas:
For the Master of the Transformation, it is thus, it is thus. When attained within the mind, even the *eranda* tree becomes a sandalwood tree; it is not otherwise, it is not otherwise.

Alas! To miss the essential meaning is to turn the garden of ambrosia into a field of thorns. When one decisively cuts off the patriarchs' intent right before one's face, one steps with faith upon the Buddha’s Chan.
Puhua erected the Dharma banner amidst the dust of the mundane world; Xuansha established the school’s tenets upon a fishing boat.
This is what is meant by "the place where a man of the Way travels": like fire burning ice, like an arrow leaving the bowstring.
It is not confined to the Eastern Land; how could it be separated from the Western Heaven? Having encountered the "grass" of my own house, I ask him for a single coin.
When Dao-sentient (Yao Chanren) goes to Yongjia, he does not see a single dharma—this is a great calamity. It fills the void of space, filling the ears and eyes; without cause, it suddenly turns.
A single stroke of the mechanism directly causes the stars to shift and the constellations to change. It splits open Linji’s Three Mysteries;
the wind stirs the reeds on both banks. The adamantine eye protrudes; the whale gives birth to its offspring at the bottom of the sea.
When the old monk maintains it in this way, it is forged from a single fire into a golden ball. Thrown here and there with ease, it does not answer when called. He takes it back to Mount Yandang.
Before the Peak, beat the drum and call for all to assemble; look and see!
Sending off the attendant of Jingci, he returned once more to Baizhang and visited Master Ma.
All his skillful means were exhausted; a single shout left him deaf for three days. At such a critical moment, one must awaken with fierce resolve.
If one says that "smelting the great metal" is precisely the sickness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, then Master Wujin closed his scroll and refused to believe it.
Miaoxi, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, is the authentic eye for all time; Yun'an and Sixin have already settled the matter through their guidance.
The call and response proceed in tandem; the rhythm and beat correspond well. One who raises it once immediately knows the sound; only upon touching the knee does one begin to show reverence.
Majestic is the Linji lineage, standing like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high. The Three Mysteries raise the banner of the Dharma; even the thousand sages dare not approach.
Treading upon the highest barrier, he sits firmly at the summit of Vairocana. Vast and open like empty space, brilliant as the sun and moon together.
Those who speak of "two or three" or "four or seven" cannot avoid playing with shadows and light. The superior man’s faculty is sharp; the needle in the bag has finally emerged from its sheath.
In years past, I ascended Nanping; my journey was not in vain. As if extinguishing a fire upon my head, I strove directly against every fleeting moment.
Having accepted the challenge beneath the shout, I also attained deep realization through the staff. Where there is courtesy, there is joy; where there is a call, there is an answer.
Neither side shall be at fault; all enter the Great Perfect Mirror. This practice should be investigated further to continue the compassionate life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
To the Zen student Hengbo:
Huangbo was a grandmotherly old woman, and Dayu was a loquacious fellow. Although the Buddha-dharma is not much, it is truly like cutting through nails and severing iron.
Indeed, to directly accept and take responsibility for this is like a flake of snow upon a red furnace; inside and out it is pure and uniform, penetrating above, below, and in all four directions.
To reach through to the year ahead and pull back the tiger’s whiskers will surely be like a clap of thunder and a flash of lightning.
With the mechanism of the iron ox, the Ancestor’s Heart-Seal seals the mud, seals the water, and seals the void. Letting forth the lion’s roar within the sandalwood grove—
Playing with the moon, speaking of the moon, pointing to the moon—this was sent to the Head Seat Duangiang of Jingci Temple, the foremost among the assembly at Nanping Mountain.
With a single stroke of his head, he transcends all quarters; it is just like Shaoyang seeing Lingyun.
The tree: Entrusted with the Great Dharma, he upholds the fundamental principles of the school. At times, having borrowed the seat of the Highest Realm, he no longer bows to the King of Mount Sumeru.
Holding the whisk in his hand, he prepares to suspend the rope-bed as he proclaims the teaching. When the wind comes, the grass must surely bow;
when the arrow is not yet released, the occasion itself is forgotten. The blind donkey extinguishes the Eye of the True Dharma; the precious sword is chillingly sharp.
A piercing cold light arises; it startles the multitude and terrifies the crowd, making it impossible to avoid.
Suddenly, Nanquan takes his seat, leaving Wang Lao’s sharp wit with no recourse but to descend to the lower level and patrol the hall.
To Master Xiuyin, Secretary of Jingci:
"The Master did not know how to read; Bodhidharma did not understand Chan. There is the thorny chestnut to swallow and the diamond ring to pass through."

Neither swallowed nor penetrated—once it strikes, it must be foremost. Like writing characters in the dark, though the full meaning of the characters may not be complete, one attains mastery in both vertical and horizontal strokes, and the brilliance of the composition already shines forth.
In days of yore, the Elder Huanglong bore the burden of the Dharma with firm intellectual power.

In the dead water of Letan, he soaked his nostrils until they were pierced through. In a fit of rage, he threw his pillow at Old Yue, yet he had not yet forgotten the distinction between the orthodox and the deviant.
Suddenly he came to see Ciming, and with a single word, he cast off the shackles of his limitations. He was like gold refined a hundred times, its color bright and radiant when bent around a finger.
Illuminating the great trichiliocosm, the moon of the mind is ever solitary and full. A man of spirit should seek this out; in every action, he should strive to emulate the sages.

All the more so when holding aloft the torch of wisdom—one’s conduct should be such that one can clasp their shoulders. Without needing to stand at the three barriers, go straight before the time of Vimalacitra.
Sending off Yun, the Abbot, as he returns to his former retreat:
Clouds emerge from the mountain peaks with no fixed intent; water fills its hollows and flows on. Upon encountering a high mountain it must stop;
reaching the great ocean, only then does it rest. To know when to stop is what is noble; if one does not stop, where else can one seek? From head to tail, traversing the three realms.
Standing upright, four directions: eastward and westward, ten thousand *li* without a blade of grass. Qin did not care, Han did not take it up;
it breaks forth from the head of Yunmen’s staff. Five thousand scrolls face this single word—how could speech and silence ever exhaust its source?
Were it otherwise, how could there be the Three Mysteries and Essentials of Linji, the Four Kinds of Discernment, and the profound mystery of the direct pointing to what is above?

It was halted above by a great wind. It has simply reached its ultimate extent throughout heaven and earth and across ten thousand ages. This talk shall be widely propagated throughout the land of China;
with mountains stretching on and waters flowing on, this merchandise that has lingered for a thousand years—where would it not be considered elegant?

The Master said to the Zen practitioners: "When you manifest as ordinary beings, you are entirely ordinary; when you manifest as sages, you are entirely sage. If the eye at the crown of your head has not yet opened, how can you distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox?
As for the old bhikṣus of the Western Heaven, they may be in samādhi or not."
Seeing off Zen-man Yuan for Jiangxi:
Throughout the ten directions there is no empty space; across the great earth there is not a single inch of soil. Were it not for General Li, who could recognize the tiger of the South Mountain?

Spontaneously manifesting bodies at the tips of a hundred grasses, responding to circumstances as one, two, three, four, or five; when the thread goes out and the silk comes in, the true master is tested.
There are those with copper heads and iron jaws as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. With divine mechanisms exchanged, Shi Gong draws his bow;
with rhythmic beats reciprocated, He Shan beats his drum. Startled, the Five Elders of Mount Cao’e look on as the wooden man performs his dance.

When Songmao went as an attendant scribe to Mount Jing, the Golden-colored Dhūta discussed kalpas while sitting in meditation. Since then, what have you been seeking by knocking at this door? He further said:
"To go up Mount Jing—to open one's mouth is already to fall into error. For the truth to flow forth from one’s own breast is still considered casual; to seek it outwardly is truly not permissible."
Have you not seen it? A single thought tied to the slightest hair is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting emotion arises and one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas.

When not even a speck of dust remains, one returns home. Let me further explain this from the beginning: Before Bodhidharma had yet arrived, when did such a thing ever exist? Neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs could fathom it;
throughout antiquity and the present, it has been treated as a stagnant commodity. "Three pounds of flax on the scale"—the thief is but a petty person.
To act: to sit squarely at the head and cut it off, there is no room for deliberation. When the snow-song and the *bāgē* are sung, there is one who joins in.
Sending off a Zen practitioner: the phoenix dances in the azure sky; the tortoise drills through the wall; sweeping past two layers of barriers; swallowing the thorny chestnut while enduring death.

Iron walls and silver mountains soar ten thousand fathoms high; look at the sun rising from the eastern side.
Inscription for the "One Strike" Studio:

Though those who have attained it call it the highest of high-level capacities (*uttamottama-yāna*), those of inferior roots ultimately consider it but empty words. While it is indeed difficult to learn the Way through mere erudition, when cognitive awareness is suddenly forgotten— [...the true state is revealed.]

In antiquity there was one whose essence was tranquil; though bound by the dust of the world, his nature remained perfectly round. Within the dharmas of sense-faculties and objects, what need is there to cling?

When a man of the Way plants tall bamboos before his window—if he does not plant this "Gentleman," others call him vulgar. In what year did he clear away the pebbles and strike at the empty tips of the branches?

Carving out large squares for his inscriptions, he pursued the fragrant footsteps of the ancients. Droplets of rain are like *śukti* pearls, each drop perfectly round; swaying in the wind, the phoenix-tail leaves form clusters of lush green. Thus it is with human life...
Wandering monks value the correctness of their vision; I recognize the man of the Way, and my own mind is naturally satisfied. It is not merely that I cherish the "head-word" of Nanyang;
when the moment arrives, I wish to transcend even manifold blessings. When a guest comes to see the noticeboard, they must see the person; seeing the person, they must understand the true standard.
The Head Seat is sent forth with this instruction:

Before the sound fades, there is no room for deliberation; after the phrase ends, it becomes ever more subtle and dense. Step by step, one treads upon the cold frost; the staff sprouts two wings.

The spiritual source surges with water; the myriad phenomena naturally sink away. Not a single speck of dust moves; there is host and guest, there is seizing and letting go.
Releasing two and casting three aside, he holds up the staff alone and plays with it. Planting flowers upon a rock, seeking a seam in empty space—three before and three after.

The great gate of giving opens wide—eighteen unshared qualities, impartial and boundless, vast and empty through and through.
Following the teaching, at the tip of Deshan’s staff, a drop of water freezes solid. Suddenly twisting his face, he catches the seeker and gives him a push. Thus do the Buddhas and Patriarchs act.

where, in the end, does the phrase return? Just as we hear that Daba has arrived, he is already heading for Mount Yangshan once more—three thousand [miles]."
The peach tree blooms in the spring. A nine-thousand-li journey for the *páng* bird soars with ease. One drags a stone; two carry earth. With a confident step, one treads upon Mount Sumeru.
Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations. With a single gulp, one drinks dry the waters of the West River. *Duò duò duò!
Lì wéi xī!* The superior practitioner applies themselves diligently; those of middling and inferior capacity do not rejoice upon hearing this. Behold the turning of the pearl.
When the jade wheel turns, the Correct and the Deviant are simultaneously raised together.

To the Zen practitioner, he says: "Tsk! What thing is this? The supreme man among superiors is stubbornly subjected to humiliation. It is like encountering a nail in barren ground; it is like a thunderclap in a clear blue sky. Even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot [avoid it].
The same path. What gain or loss is there between ancient and modern? At every turn, the sea moon and mountain clouds; everywhere, green, red, and intermingled with blue.
Cast aside the "tortoise-nose snake" of Nanshan: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.
The staff of the Chan master of Tiantai and Yunchu rises like clouds;
the flower in his alms-bag pouch blooms. Having traversed a hundred cities, he departs to roam the peaks of Tiantai and Yunchu.
The rocks are jagged and the white waters flow vast; the flowers fall petal by petal as brocade-like clouds blaze with color. He swallows the acorn-bushes of Yangqi and laughs at Muzhou.
Bearing the board of the province, he continued the true lamp of Shaoshi and opened the orthodox eye for humans and devas. Have you not seen?
When he manifested as Hanshan, he alone swept the pine gate, thereby causing the three-lifetime habitual tendencies of Dayang to be forgotten;
when our Ancestor Caoxi sat grandly upon his high seat, he crushed Yongjia’s pride as he circled the bed with his staff raised.
In "Self-Pastoral" (Jimok), he shows the Way to the Chan practitioner named Geum (Kyeom);
his pen-name is Jimok. To pasture oneself by means of the Way, there is nothing that is not sufficient. One should know that this Way emerges from the natural;
how could its enjoyment ever fail to be mature? The water-buffalo of Mount Mui touches the east and then touches the west—thus it is.

Thirty years have passed; year after year the stream-side grass turns green. On the south bank and the north bank, the spring breeze blows; before the mountains and behind the mountains, the sun lingers slow.
Lying across or reclining prostrate—truly a life of ease! How could this meaning be allowed for others to know?
Tomorrow morning he is let loose, yet as before he is led back home. The tethering rope is cast down and he sits upon his own back; look at him when his nostrils point toward the vast heavens!
Seeing Attendant Chao off on his way home:
The attendant has attained Zen, yet lacks skillful means when facing critical moments. Amidst a thousand or ten thousand people, who is it that cannot see?
The third watch moon shines through the window; at noon, the wind blows upon the face. Extinguish the Shaolin lineage—what prevents a single thread from passing through?
Morning and evening, one must return; time passes as swiftly as lightning.
In the same rhyme, I see off Chan-man Zhao as he returns to attend upon Master Xugu of Yangshan.

The various elders of Jiangxi are like a vast, overflowing stream; among them, eighty-four men do not suffice to count them all. Yet, when compared, it is Yangshan who possesses even a fraction of their essence.
I have heard that in recent years his tongue has grown worn thin. You are now returning to pursue a second visit; once you reach his gate, pray extend my greetings for me.
Homage. Having finished tailoring the hundred-patch *kāṣāya*, I have planted more pine and cypress trees at the edge of my hut.

To the Zen practitioner Dongchan, I show that the true mechanism of Shaoshi changes even at midday: when the dark moon hides, the white moon appears; the luminous pearl that settles the sea remains entirely as it is.
Like a golden bird atop the summit, swift as an arrow; Chan Master Daoxin attained it with ease. With a single hand he pulled away Mount Sumeru;
the Yellow River surged and Mount Hua split asunder. A lion crouched upon the earth as clouds and waves overturned;
Old Man Dongchan slept in the Triangle. To recognize this fellow is truly not mistaken. Wall-contemplation has passed nine springs; one flower, five petals.
The leaves open and then fall.
To see off the Head Seat Yishou returning to Sichuan to visit his mother:
"A dog has no Buddha-nature. When asked, he immediately responds; a single phrase is precisely appropriate. He strips away the maladies of Buddhas and patriarchs.
This is the eye at the crown of the stream of Chan; its light shines brilliantly, illuminating earth and heaven.

Traveling ten thousand miles from the south, it has reached here without moving a foot, yet everything is clearly discerned. Dongshan attained this and arranged it into the five ranks of ruler and subject;
Linji employed it and divided it into four kinds of critical examinations. There are Yangqi’s "diamond circle" and "thorny chestnut," and Baiyun’s...
Add where there is excess and subtract where there is deficiency. When it comes to old Dongshan, he bites through the iron-acid preserves;

he sells three *jin* of "weighed-to-the-scale" hemp to those who carry a shoulder-board. This is a transformation beyond the ordinary, with a thousand variations and ten thousand distinctions—truly many paths. Yet, for those of wondrous, perfect, and transcendent realization, it is directly present and complete;
there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation. Simply take this very thing and offer it to the Honored Hall to benefit all people.
What limits can there be to the heavens?
I see Master Jia returning to Caoxi in Yongjia;
who has truly transmitted the Heart-Seal? It is said that after staying for a single night, he reached the ultimate depth. By inquiring into the reason for this, one comes to recognize it.
End. Three times he circumambulated the meditation seat and shook his golden staff. Regarding the great matter of birth and death, there is nothing that can be done.

To open one’s mouth is to lose it; to keep the mouth shut is to lose it as well. The three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand practices—sixty minor kalpas have passed like a swift wind and rain.

Rest, rest, rest! Counting grains of sand and pouring them into the sea is but a weary toil. Return to the Pines-and-Wind Pavilion and gaze at the river moon. This is the talk of an old man who has retired from the world.
Wu She sent this to the Chan Master Rui, the Librarian of the Five Patriarchs Monastery, saying:
"To speak of Chan is to engage in evil speech. If you are a true follower of the Way, you should firmly uphold these words."
