When applying the Dharma in response to the occasion, every step transcends the old molds. This is called the Gate of Perfect Penetration; when has it ever established doors or windows?
This refers to that which is not a gate of perfect penetration; such a statement is also unacceptable. It would mean being born before Maitreya and dying after Gautama.
From today until tomorrow morning—clearly, three, eight, and nine.
To Yunju’s Abbot Yu, I present these four staff-blows beneath Mount Jiyun.
A great Zen Buddha of the world, a Lord of Peace within the mountains of Yunju—what person would dare to treat him with contempt?
With one blow, the two secure gates are flung open; like a falcon soaring through the void against the sun, it soars across the vast heavens. The void...

Understanding this, one bursts into laughter. Ten thousand phenomena vie with one another in their abrupt emergence. The stone man’s sash is wide, exposing his backbone. Have you not seen Old Xuefeng?
He held up the essential principles of the school with such directness before others. Nan-shan’s turtle-nosed snake spat forth poisonous breath, so terrifying that Shao-yang had nowhere to hide.
Now it is hidden beneath Dulong Bridge; let those who come cast a discerning eye upon it.

Not obscured. Before leaving Tuṣita to descend into the royal palace, he was truly the foremost among gods and humans. From beneath his tongue, the blue lotus fragrance wafts richly;

The white ox stands revealed in the open field, yet cannot be borne away; it is cast into the fragrant grasses of the Snowy Mountains. Return!
Before the land of South India, the eyes cannot see through it, yet the ears may transmit it. Otherwise, listen further as I, Xiujū, explain it in detail:
it cuts off the tracks and paths of both the holy and the ordinary.
Seeing off Chan Master Po as he departs for Nanshan—down the slope he does not run;
such a swift opportunity is hard to encounter again. Holding high the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he awakens the blind and the deaf.
His own spiritual powers and samādhi are applied boundlessly at every turn. He divides the splendor of Mount Taihua that reaches the heavens and soars upon the whirlwind of ninety thousand *li*.
The wind that exhausts the surging waves of the ocean of suffering; the clearing away of the tracks of various creatures in the dense forest. Having kicked over the lame donkey, where has it gone?
The southern mountain burns charcoal, and the northern mountain glows red.

When the "thorny chestnut" is flung out, one swallows it whole. The myriad dharmas proliferate, arising and ceasing of their own accord; Who says that a hungry gut has ever been satisfied?

A clamor—like the wind passing by the ear. That Nanyue and Qingyuan attained what they did was truly for a reason.

To this day, the stream of Cao has been drained to its bottom, without a drop of water remaining. You should now go alone and not question others; to question others is to see waves and billows arise.
Furthermore, he spoke of a single outstanding colt that tramples all people underfoot; since when has there ever been a "self"?
He named the room where the Head Seat resided "True Illumination" (Zhenzhao) and requested a verse with a preface for it:

"True Illumination is manifest before one; illusory phenomena are simultaneously stilled. Since illusory phenomena are stilled, True Illumination is also empty. When both the real and the illusory are absent," [the verse concludes].
The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs can thus be approached. Therefore, the marvel lies in embodying what precedes:
tranquil yet ever-illuminating, unmoving from the fundamental limit, yet pervading the midst of worldly toil. This is why this new structure at Xuyan bears the name "Southern Chu."
This was not composed in vain. The recluse Xiujū praised what he had been called and spoke a verse, saying:
"Within the great void of space, all phenomena are contained. Nature and wisdom are wondrously perfect, devoid of any marks of discrimination. Thus one observes the ten directions."
Like a jewel held in the palm, the subject and object of cognition transcend all measurement; true illumination is boundless.
Whether in the human realm or the heavens, what demonic spirit has sent you, student and attendant, back to receive instruction?
What demonic spirit has taught you to leave the household life and study the Way? A man’s departure from home must be undertaken by himself.
Be strong! Be careful not to let your body enter the wild weeds. When an attendant attains Zen, a single blow is enough to bring it to an end.
The three thousand lands and seas become empty; the ten billion Mount Sumerus are small. Once empty space has vanished, the myriad phenomena have nowhere to be sought.
Open the eye atop the crown of Mahesvara; reveal the treasure within your own robe. Vast and expansive, yet not external—this is the secret of the Vulture Peak.
Entrusted with the radiance of the sense-base of touch, it is desolate and not within; yet one must strive to inherit the ancestral fields and gardens.
When the attendant Dan was sent to visit the Master’s travels of over a thousand li, how could he have ever sold his cotton robe? He preserved the warmth throughout his entire body and returned.
I pay deep reverence to the Master’s countenance. This is my own fine son; though one beats him, he cannot be killed. Were this another’s horse, it would be difficult to ride.

He whips the golden cock and brushes the jade hare; he turns the axis of the earth and revolves the pivot of heaven. Only after administering three severe blows straight down will one know that the tiger’s body is naturally striped.
Sending Attendant Quan to Visit the Master (four people traveling together):
Four people on one boat, brothers joined by the character for "ten. Each is unaware of the others; even Buddhas and Patriarchs are like this.
How much more so for those who have spent three years at Lake Tan—picking up their spoons and setting down their chopsticks, they are all exactly the same.

When the total capacity of the mechanism is applied, where has there ever been a fundamental tenet? To tear apart Mount Taihua is merely to flaunt one’s prowess; to pass through the Dragon Gate, who could burn off their own tail?
Return before the Master and try to display it; even traveling a thousand li and circling a hundred times, it is difficult to evade.

As old age and illness have long persisted, I have had no mind to handle brush and ink. Yet, my attendant Yin came before me with paper in his sleeve, seeking a verse to accompany him on his journey back to Zhejiang.
Fortunately, there is that former arrow-splitting mechanism; carelessly brought forth, it is the foremost swiftness. "I am not as good as you"—the sword has long since departed;
why mark the boat? I dare say you have not yet reached the bottom: like a numinous tortoise dragging its tail, you merely manifest shadows and traces.
Last night at the third watch, the ox was lost; at dawn, having risen, the thief was caught. *Duḥ!* (A shout of realization).
Inscription for the Portrait of the Monk Chuanshi:
A wind of purity for all ages. A single oar is his livelihood; there are no fish upon the water, yet there is bait on the hook. To dwell here is not like dwelling elsewhere.
If it is like this, then there is no dwelling. Nodding his head three times, he said, "There is no need for further deliberation. Where has the boatman gone after capsizing the vessel?
To the Layman Chen Zhenming (who named the room where he dwelt "The Water-Moon Dharma Hall"), the Layman Zhenming sought the True School.
As the years and months passed, he forgot his own efforts; a single mote of dust flew up and obscured the heavens.

Black! He sweeps away the myriad phenomena, distinguishing east from west. Sometimes he sits in repose within the moon reflected in water, able to cause the six faculties and their worldly afflictions to become empty.
Cultivating a livelihood and engaging in industry are but secondary matters; looking left and right, he opens the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf.

When day breaks upon the mountain peak, the jade hare emerges; at midnight beneath the ocean floor, the golden crow is crimson. A flute without holes, a lute without strings—when the melody is high, it naturally possesses its own resonance.
People know his fame; when Kāśyapa heard the sound of the bamboo shoots, he once rose to dance. His habitual tendencies were not yet eliminated, yet he succeeded our Patriarch.

The wind stirs and dust flies from the ocean floor; the clouds part and the moon appears in the midst of heaven.

Free from names and free from forms, the Three Essentials and Three Mysteries transcend both speech and silence, manifesting the Real and the Expedient. He brandishes forth the rhinoceros fan; its pure breeze reveals its complete majesty.
Where is there a long river without white waves? Whose hearth has no blue smoke?
Bestowing the "Vajra Ring" and "Thorny Jujube" upon Head Seat Lu—when brought forth, they terrify the old man of the eastern village. Head Seat Lu in the mountains of Siming.
This perspective is not like that of ordinary people. Relying on a celestial long sword held firmly in hand, it suddenly hangs upside down between the two eyebrows.
Severing his own arm in his quest for the Dharma, he laughed at the Second Patriarch, who did not understand how to skillfully conceal his blade.

The intimate eye of humans and devas; the secret pivot of Buddhas and patriarchs. A pearl threaded through a nine-bend needle; jade split by a ring-saw.
Behold the four rattan canes—what could compare to their functional efficacy? The great Chan Buddhas of the world nod their heads in self-approval.
From where does the Indian monk come? He reveals his coarse and vulgar bearing. With fists raised and feet kicked up, he perfectly accords with the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Two mouths yet not a single tongue; he stubbornly claims there is a fundamental principle. How could this reach the state of spontaneity? Neither taking away nor bestowing.
Just as when Master Shaoyang traveled to Lingshu, a single phrase perfectly coincided with the truth; it has been broadcast through the ears of people for a thousand ages.
A towering banner of radiance—watch as it is raised and established before our very eyes.
Seeing off Chief Seat Chi as he returns to Zhejiang to part ways—parting ways!
How can this matter be described? Meeting him three thousand miles away makes the mountain clouds and ocean moon burst into laughter.

In the Buddha-dharma, one does not concern oneself with existence or non-existence; it is simply a matter of being direct and immediate at the very head. Thus, ten thousand manifestations flow forth spontaneously.

parting, parting. Why not speak of this matter? When meeting, one values only the true knower. It must be clear and direct.

A mountain dweller in his true colors, yet without a trace of axe or hatchet marks. He brings forth this one move and shatters the broken sand-pot.

His words are as warm as spring, his spiritual mechanism as swift as a flash of lightning. Do not remain as a mere scavenger.
Eating rice with the mouth; one does not understand how to chew it finely, but swallows it whole. At midnight a thief is caught; at dawn the gate is firmly closed.
Tell this to Old Uncle Wang of the mountain front; let him listen and enter the deep village with a smile.

The void falls to the earth; sun and moon turn black. Iron walls and silver mountains—how oppressive they are! Suddenly, with one step, the heavens and earth are vast and wide. Why is it so difficult to see through the eight facets of this translucent clarity?
An Inscription for Layman Li, with Preface.
Layman Tingzuo is a bodhisattva practicing Prajñā while remaining in the household.

Seek it within the midst of worldly toil; you must grasp it firmly and become its master with fierce intensity.

Even when confronted by a thousand hardships and ten thousand conflicting circumstances, if you can illuminate them through the principle of emptiness, then the wondrous, pure, and perfectly enlightened nature will naturally become vast, transparent, and pervasive in all places, and your majestic power will be sovereign. He then spoke a verse:

Amidst the dust and toil of worldly afflictions, all-pervading is the nature of emptiness. When not a single thought arises, one is primordially pure. There is no dharma to be sought and no mind to be realized.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether moving or resting, one is empty within and compliant without. Thus, one penetrates beyond birth and death and subdues both the heterodox and the orthodox.
For this reason, Pang Gong transcended the mundane and entered the sacred. I know that my assistant Ting’s spiritual capacity is sharp and keen;

even while within the burning house, he did not seek fame or reputation. Did he not marry off his sons and give away his daughters? Amidst the myriad affairs of the world, his body and mind remained vast and serene.
Contemplating the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, one awakens to fundamental wisdom. In the past, Vimalakīrti was neither one nor two;

whether in Jambudvīpa in the south or Aparagoyānī in the west, the patriarchs’ mind-seal is like the mechanism of the iron ox. As a model for future generations, it can only be known through personal realization.
To do what is not to be done, and to act for what is not to be acted upon; to break free from the nest and the mortar—this moment is fleeting.
Should these words be forgotten, Shen may record them here.

I show that the Chan practitioner does not long for the sages and does not prize their own spiritual brilliance. Only when the myriad functions have all ceased is the person of original nature revealed:
majestic and dignified, with the mark upon the crown of the head;磊磊落落 (leileiluo), a celestial qilin. The rooster does not eat food earned by no merit. Left.
The eyes weigh eight *liang*. A hawk does not strike a rabbit by the hedge. The right eye weighs half a *jin*. Plucking the willow blossoms—plucking the willow blossoms!
Do not rashly take action three thousand miles away. Having made the vow, I have never scattered sand since.
Addressing the junior master Yongyuan, the Rector, [the Master] said:
"The utterance is not sound; the Brahma-voice is pure and elegant, yet no one hears it. Form is not a thing before the eyes; it appears and vanishes in vain within the realm of the five turbidities.
Drawing forth the golden mallet from the sleeve, he smashes the nest of right and wrong. Xinghua struck Kebin; this is the mountain..."
The ghost seizes the celestial qilin; he is fined and driven out of the monastery. The Śākyamuni Buddha does not sit upon the Palace of the Empty King;
neither is he struck nor is he fined. After years of arduous toil, one must wear socks. When a single word is uttered before birth, a pure breeze rises from the ends of heaven.
Reaching the peaks and the mountains, its momentum cannot be turned back; piercing the willow at a hundred paces, the arrow—
Not in vain was this laughter; it topples the Buddha of the Future as he descends to birth. This is precisely like a blind man stumbling about in the dark.
*Duh!* (A cry of reproach). An Epilogue for the Late Master Yuet-lam Yuk-tong:
Upon receiving the news of the passing of Master Yuet-lam Yuk-tong, his final verse at the time of death stated: "Eighty-three years—what [is there to say]?"
The patriarchs have become Buddhas; the void has fallen to the ground. His remains were cremated, yet his teeth remained distinct and uncorrupted;
the *śarīra* relics were brilliantly radiant. Thereupon, he spoke a verse in lamentation, saying:
The day space fell to the earth has long since passed; the cypress seedling surpasses Maitreya.

Upon the cliff-stones by the waters of the Long Ditch, a great mass of fire blossoms with golden lotuses. This verse of wind-bone never revealed in his lifetime—where can one find it when the teeth are struck?
Suddenly, the *śarīra* bursts forth; why so much as eight pecks and four bushels?
Seeing off the Abbot of the Repository, Caima, as he returns to Siming with the Great Canon and the Small Canon:
both have emerged from this very place; when even the harmony itself is overturned, go straight to question Maitreya.
Coming, it does not traverse the path; going, it leaves no trace. A single phrase settles the fundamental principle, surpassing hundreds of thousands of billions.
The water-buffalo of Mount Gui: though slaughtered, the dog will not eat it.
Zen practitioner Xieze Shan Woshang requested a response to his poem "The Idler’s Song.
Whether idle or busy, look at it: neither concerns the heart-mind. To go about in idleness is like ripples upon the water.
In moments of busyness, I repeatedly find treasures within my robes; though my horns are not yet fully grown, I wander aimlessly with the current.
As soon as one enters the wasteland, who can distinguish the weeds? The two characters "right" and "wrong" arise without root; with a single word of "good" or "evil," everything is understood.
It is well to be idle, it is well to be busy. An idle person speaks to a busy person: "Hurry on and chase after things—turn your head back early! Behold the mountains of the Five Lakes."
The Sea Island: The nostrils have always hung downward; when you cannot grasp them, cease seeking elsewhere.
To Master Xing:
For three years Xing has been by my side; he has naturally attained the daily functioning of his own life. In response to a monk’s question regarding characters, I do not seek them out.
Constantly, like lightning rolling and stars racing, there is but a single point; at dawn, with a blink of an eye, it is to the east of the river.
Summer clouds unfurl and fold over many wondrous peaks; the cypress tree before the courtyard attains Buddhahood, shattering the void as it stands tall and imposing.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner to Nanhua to pay homage to the Patriarchs:
the sacred traces of the Master are everywhere throughout the human world; why should they be limited to Nanhua and Mount Yue? Picking through the weeds, the golden robe appears tattered;
striking the stone, the sound of "Wang Shanshan" rings out. The mountain-shape staff is lean as a horned dragon; Sinu’s eighth-generation robe is worn like a tiger.
There are speckles. Returning another day, he leans against a courtyard tree and laughs as he watches a thousand peaks rise in waves.
Seeing off a Chan practitioner to Yongjia to pay respects at the Master’s stupa:
"With empty hands, he brought along a dull iron spade; who would have known there were billows beneath his feet? He intends to seek out the sacred bones to bury his head."

Entering, his entire body was already engulfed in flames; lying down, he listened as the pine wind blew against the eaves of the house. Sitting, he watched as the river moon shifted around the mountain’s waist.
In the assembly at Mount Pan, he performed a somersault; for a thousand ages, he surpasses Puhua in loftiness.
Following the rhyme of Master Dongzhou of Huqiu, I present this verse to layman Chen, who is establishing a reception hall and five bridges for the northern Water-and-Clouds Community.
Ordinary and sages pass through like rice and hemp; Since we cook rice with no grain, We must diligently serve tea to test those who come.
The Patriarchal Master’s instruction should be the beginning; The completion of this great undertaking rests upon the Elder.
In an instant, with a single snap of the fingers, one ascends to the realm of Gandhavyūha. A great rain of sweet nectar falls, nourishing the sprouts upon the fiery mountain.
When will I go alone to the hall on the west bank to sever [delusions]? In how many days shall I revisit the Ten-Li Lake? Lately, there have been many teachers at Nandang.
Very well. At the end of the day, I see that my travels have been in vain. Heaven and earth age me; I have but three rooms.
My old ties are clear, yet I am estranged from others by half a scroll of writing. Last night the north wind rose from the very ground; a heap of yellow leaves fills the cold stove.
Inscription for the Ichishoku-kken (Single-Color Pavilion):
Ten-thousand-li clear skies immerse the jade pitcher; one knows not where the level marshes begin. A flying white bird vanishes into the clarity;
gazing toward the azure heavens, they end in nothingness. The world beneath one’s eyes is as vast as this; yet of human affairs, past and present, there remains naught.
Part One: Long ago, before the birth of the Buddha—A single tune of a fisherman’s song falls upon Lake Duan.
Two Verses in Mourning for Master Dongzhou, written on the nineteenth day of the third month in the Gui-chou year:
At Yunyan, he fully manifested the body of the Dharma King; Before one’s very eyes, he pointed out Bodhi.

When the discourse reaches the Dharma-body having no dwelling place, one finally knows that the myriad phenomena alone claim supremacy. The old oyster of the playful waves has been pregnant for a thousand years;

Seeing off the Chan practitioner for Mount Jing: Suzhou has it, and Changzhou has it; yet there is even more at Lingxiao above them all. That "biting the arrowhead" device is still dull;
the three blows given to others are but a light recompense. The azure sky unfolds like a dimming painting; the waters of the grotto flow on in a surging torrent.
The current flows upstream; it is always manifest before one's eyes. Seizing it, one blocks off several throats.

Narrow! It surges toward the heavens; let the head hang low. How could high mountains obstruct the gathering of phoenixes? Only dense forests provide a place for birds and sparrows to roost.
Once the money for rice gruel, water, and straw sandals has been paid, we shall come together to eat some coarse porridge.
Director Yang visited me to hear the Dharma;

How joyful it is that the lineage of the Great Year remains; together we shall follow in the ancient footsteps of Master Pang.
The wind returns; naturally, the gateway of one's circle of acquaintances is small. What need is there to decline meeting you? A single snap of the fingers.
Sending this Chan practitioner back to Yongjia to visit his kin:
in the hall, both parents have their hair turned entirely white. The passing waves surge and surge toward the east; as the tide rises at the wild ferry, one thinks of Huangbo.
Bai. Like the long spring breeze at Puchang, one thinks of Muzhou. On this day, the toil and labor can finally be repaid; sitting much upon the ground of the mind, one must continue to cultivate.
Before Yongjia sang the tune of returning home, he once stayed for a single night at Caoxi.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Shi to Jingshan:
When genuine practice is brought to fruition, the ancient style remains pure beyond three thousand *li*. Originally there are no stages, so how could there be any falling away?
Even if you possess a sharp wit, there is no need to display it. Mazu sent over the subtle "perfect circle" (*yuánxiàng*); Master Qin pointed it out for all to see.
It is not a light matter; I do not know how one could be so deluded. Is this not like striking ice within fire?
To encounter the Rector at Donglin after traveling three thousand li—suddenly meeting again. He picks up that year’s “thorny chestnut” (lìjìpéng); it is neither lessened nor increased.

The southern mountains diminish as they burn charcoal, while the northern peaks glow red. The Poyang River carries the moon across waves a thousand fathoms deep; Mount Lu offers its view from the Five Elders’ Peak.
It is said that Master Huiyuan once formed a monastic society there; now a fragrant breeze blows over the white lotuses in the pond.

Beyond the lake, the frost is cold and the rain has just ceased. With whom will you share the boat on the Zhejiang River? Of all things, there is nothing beneath the monk’s robe;
Not a single thing exists at the tip of the staff. Baizhang went deaf because he hung up his whisk; Yanguan’s fan was broken—yet what happened then?
A bull is required. Have you ever known that these two paths do not intersect? For a thousand ages, the waters of Longyuan have flowed backward.

Sent to Shangyin, the late Master Xitang was stammering and could not speak; yet who would say his spirit and will did not swallow up all quarters? When empty space falls to the ground, it becomes itself.
The Buddha: Even when a cypress seed is burned, it still has fragrance.

When the Tripitaka was sent from Goryeo to the Jade Hall and Pearl Pavilion, all were fully opened. The Prince of Goryeo came to deliver the scriptures; as for the very first phrase, no one [can grasp it].
Meeting. What matters have been transmitted throughout the nine realms?

How is it that the various masters of transformation on all paths have brought their teachings to harmonize with the affairs of Vaiśālī? It is well to entrust gain and loss to Vimalakīrti; there is no mind in giving, nor is there no mind.
Receiving it—its thousand-year-old elegance cannot be worn away.
Old Shi of Huangmei has a sword between his brows; Dou Ba’s robe is worn through, yet he wears the talisman behind his elbow.
I too have no dharma for others; I simply hang a vinegar jar upon the wall.
Boiling sand to prepare an offering for the Tathāgata’s meal—who says the Fragrant Accumulation Hall is only in the upper realms? Cast aside the maladies of the Buddhas and Patriarchs at Vaiśālī;
every mote of dust and every land is a bridge to liberation.
Once the conditions for transformation are fulfilled, it is fitting to retire; why need one go to the slippery stone? Rarely does one encounter in this world a guest with pierced ears;
before others, it is difficult to raise the ox that passed through the window.
Watching the monk pass away while seated, he immediately gathered dry firewood and piled it into a heap; sitting there, he watched as the red flames surged from all four sides.
Indeed, he has blinded the eyes of the people of the entire city. He gathers a stalk of thatch and plants it upon a stone.
When Master Huyan of Chengtian lay ill and had no place to rise, his body was restored to health.
When medicine proves efficacious, one naturally forgets its prohibitions.
On what day will he alone lead thirty thousand followers, scattering flowers as they come to circle the Master’s bed?
An Imitation of the Ten Verses of Fenyang, with Preface:
While staying in a guest room on Mount Feng, I once again read the verses and sayings of Master Fenyang.

Among them, there are ten pieces—ranging from "Discerning the Deviant and the Correct" to "Praising the Master’s Spiritual Faculties"—each with its own title. Observing the intent behind their composition, they are truly the skillful means of a patriarchal teacher.

Interspersing guidance with the three mysteries and piecing together the five ranks, he was able to enable students to prune away obstructions and penetrate the fundamental source, transcending all conceptual measurements without fail.
Alas! The times have surely reached their decline, and the faculties of men have become increasingly dull.

Not only am I unable to investigate its ultimate purpose, but there are few who can cause others to develop deep faith in the Buddhas and patriarchs of the past, who bestowed compassion and provided vast salvation for such great benefit.
Nevertheless, disregarding my own ignorance and mediocrity, I have ventured to emulate the practices of former masters by composing ten verses myself.
I have composed this general verse to leave behind for you, my two or three disciples, so that you may find encouragement therein.

To distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, one must know the essential points of the Master who proclaims the school. To discern the heterodox from the orthodox, one must examine the capacity of those who come; the eye atop the head resides within the eyebrows.
It is already too late when you look up at the eyebrows.

Fearing a mere vague stone, one finds a piece of jade, exquisite and clear; only after it is split open does one know the skill of the craftsman. Without touching the immediate occasion, you must speak.
[The Master] said: "I tell you to cease deluding yourself regarding the master of the house.
Clever sophistry is not true;
beneath the tongue, waves and billows roll in myriads. You must know that it does not reside on the surface of the lips. Only when the banner-staff is toppled is the truth revealed."
Only then will you truly believe that there is a distinct transmission from the West,

which enables the complete integration of ordinary and sagely, noble and foolish, along a single path. The descendants of Deshan and Linji pass the thread back and forth, fully manifesting life itself.
Kill! Every drop of clarified butter (sarpis) penetrates the gate of the crown.
If you try to bring it forth, though you hold out both hands, there is not a single thing to be found. A gourd hanging from the head of a coffin—know for certain that this is no immortal.
As for technique: those who rely on the "Life-Seizing Talisman" behind their elbows merely boast in vain;
the Master of the House discerns all things, head and tail, manifesting the True Lineage. One can directly verify the wind coming from before one's eyes. Do not hesitate to extend that Nātha hand!
The Hand. As above, it strikes the *Sumeru-puditi* bell.

Recognizing the sharp point [of the teaching] is like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint—there is no room for hesitation. One must clarify the upward-tending mechanism face-to-face; the seven-star light penetrates the casket and shines brilliantly.
Decayed! How many people know how to handle a steamer?
Within the phrase, the truth is revealed;

yet as soon as one engages with verbal explanations, one has already erred. To seek it further beyond words is to go astray; only when the eyes see directly and the hands discern can one distinguish the black from the white.
Ordinary life—when has it ever not been in accord? When Emperor Xianzong used a whisk and was rebuked, he demonstrated the authentic transmission.
As soon as the eye stirs, one falls into a deep abyss; not only does one stick out the tongue in shock at the Yellow Emperor.
Huangbo. A golden-haired lion emerges from its cave, its nostrils pierced through.

Praising the Master’s function for unfolding the ancestral Way, it is called "total raising. His merit is so great it is difficult to equal that of the Creator; yet even a single blow behind the head still leaves him blinking.
Thunder. Beyond the Seven Golden Mountains, the sun’s orb descends low.
